opus-5.5.text:
I think Move 37 is such a powerful example because it captures something we don't often get to see so clearly: a system that has learned so deeply from a domain that it starts to find things outside the space of what humans would have considered. When AlphaGo played that move, the commentators thought it was a mistake. Top professionals would have put the odds of a human playing it at something like one in ten thousand. And yet it turned out to be a pivotal, creative move. It wasn't random. It came from an understanding of the game built up through enormous amounts of search and self-play.

When I think about chemistry and biology, I expect we'll see the same pattern, and in some ways it'll be even more pronounced. Go is a game humans have studied for thousands of years, so our intuitions there are quite refined. In drug design, the space of possible molecules is astronomically large, something like ten to the sixty drug-like molecules, and human chemists have explored only a tiny sliver of it. Medicinal chemists have incredible intuition, but it's shaped by what's been made before, what's easy to synthesize, and what has worked in the past. So when you build models that actually understand the physics and biology of how molecules interact with proteins, and you let them search that space, I fully expect them to propose structures and strategies that look strange to an expert at first. A chemist might look at it and say, "Why would you ever put that group there?"

The important part, and this is where the analogy gets interesting, is that in Go you find out almost immediately whether the move was brilliant: you play out the game. In biology, the feedback loop is much slower and more expensive. You have to make the molecule, test it, and eventually go through clinical trials. So the real challenge is building models accurate enough, and grounded enough in reality, that we can trust those Move 37 moments rather than dismiss them. That's why so much of the work is about getting the predictive models right, so the system's unusual ideas come from real insight rather than errors.

I also think the relationship with human experts will look a lot like what happened in Go afterward. Professional players studied AlphaGo's games and it changed how humans play. I'd love to see the same in drug discovery. These models wouldn't replace scientists' intuition. They'd expand it, showing us parts of chemical and biological space we didn't know were worth looking at. I think that's when things get really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says commentators thought Move 37 was a mistake and later calls it pivotal, but does not state that it was critical to AlphaGo’s victory.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that models will propose unusual molecular structures and strategies that initially look strange to experts, and compares these to AlphaGo’s pivotal Move 37 moments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Move 37 is, I think, the thing that I keep coming back to. For those who don't know the context, this was the second game of the match against Lee Sedol, and AlphaGo played this move on the fifth line that, if you'd shown it to a professional Go player beforehand, they'd have said it was a mistake. The commentators were genuinely confused. Lee Sedol got up and left the room for a bit. And then over the course of the next fifty or so moves it became clear this was actually a really deep, really creative move that opened up the whole board in a way no human had really considered.

And the important thing about why that happened is that AlphaGo wasn't just imitating human games. It had started by learning from human play, but then it went beyond that through self-play and reinforcement learning. It was exploring the space of possible strategies on its own, guided by the actual outcome, which is did you win the game or not. So it wasn't constrained by human intuition about what a good move looks like. It was constrained by the rules of Go and by reality.

So the question is what's the equivalent of that in chemistry and biology. And I think the analogy is pretty direct, actually. If you train a model purely on the literature, purely on the molecules humans have made and the experiments humans have run, you get something that's a very good approximation of human chemists. That's useful, but it's bounded by what we already know. The much more interesting regime is when the model gets to propose things and then gets feedback from the world. Not from a human saying this looks reasonable, but from an actual assay, an actual synthesis, an actual measurement of whether the protein folds or the compound binds. That's the win-or-lose signal.

And when you close that loop, I think you'll see Move 37 moments. You'll see the model propose a molecule or a modification or an experimental route where every medicinal chemist in the room goes, that's weird, that's not how we'd do it, that shouldn't work. And then it works. And then in hindsight you can reconstruct why, and it teaches you something about the underlying biology that you didn't have before.

The one caveat I'd put on it is that biology is a much harder game than Go in a specific way. In Go the simulator is perfect. The rules are the rules, and you can play millions of games overnight. In biology the simulator is the lab, and every move is expensive and slow and noisy. So a lot of the work right now is really about how you get that feedback loop fast enough and clean enough that the model can actually learn from its own exploration, rather than just from us. That's the bottleneck. But I don't think it's a fundamental obstacle, and I think once you crack it, the behavior you get looks a lot like what we saw on that Go board.

r001.rationale: It says observers thought Move 37 was a mistake and later describes it as deep and creative, but does not say the move was critical to AlphaGo’s victory.

r002.rationale: It predicts models will propose solutions that seem weird or wrong to human experts and then succeed.

astra-6.text:
I think Move 37 is a wonderful example of a system finding something that sits outside our intuition. You have a move that initially looks like a mistake, and then, as the game unfolds, you start to understand why it’s so powerful.

In chemistry and biology, I think we’ll see that same pattern: models proposing molecules or experiments that look strange to us because they don’t follow the patterns we’ve learned to look for. And some of those ideas could open up directions we wouldn’t otherwise have explored.

The crucial difference is that Go has very clear rules and a clear outcome. In biology, you have to go and do the experiment. So an unexpected proposal isn’t itself a breakthrough. The exciting part is connecting that creativity to experimental feedback, so we can discover which of those surprising ideas actually work.

r001.rationale: It says Move 37 initially looked like a mistake and later seemed powerful, but does not state that it was critical to AlphaGo’s victory.

r002.rationale: It predicts surprising proposals in chemistry and biology, but describes them as untested and does not clearly predict that they will be successful solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Move 37 is a beautiful example of a system finding something that was there all along, but that humans hadn’t really considered. It looked strange through the lens of human expertise, and then, as the game unfolded, its value became clear.

In chemistry and biology, I think we’ll see things with that same character: a molecule or an experiment that initially looks surprising, perhaps even wrong, because it doesn’t fit our intuition. But the important distinction is that Go has very clear rules and a definitive outcome. In biology, you have to go and do the experiment. A surprising prediction is only useful if it survives contact with the real world.

So the exciting prospect is that these models can help us move beyond the patterns we already know to look for. You want that element of surprise, coupled with a really rigorous experimental loop that tells you whether you’ve discovered something meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says Move 37 looked strange and its value later became clear, but does not say observers thought it was a mistake or that it was critical to AlphaGo’s victory.

r002.rationale: The response predicts surprising outputs that may seem wrong to human intuition, but does not clearly state that those outputs will be successful solutions; it makes their usefulness conditional on experimental validation.
